summary: Rough introductory notes arguing that network graphics protocols proposed so far are not general enough. They need to handle attention handling, picture structure and other high-level interactive graphics processes, so they can operate sophisticated systems.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 192 argues that network graphics must handle more than drawing. It discusses display differences, structured pictures and how user actions should reach the application.

subtitle: Design considerations for a flexible interactive graphics system.

tldr.problem: A graphics protocol needs to support user input and structured pictures as well as drawing commands.
tldr.mechanism: The notes propose modular software levels, support for varied displays and input devices, structured picture data and a way to report user attention to applications.
tldr.outcome: The RFC offers design considerations, not a finished protocol specification.

today: RFC 192 is a set of graphics design notes published in July 1971. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown.

sections.title: Beyond Drawing Commands
sections.content:
The author says some proposed network graphics protocols lack general mechanisms for attention handling, picture structure and other higher-level interactive functions. A useful protocol should accommodate sophisticated systems as well as simple terminals.

The RFC distinguishes storage-tube displays, which retain a drawn image, from refresh displays, which repeatedly redraw it and can support moving or selectively erased objects.
sections.plainLanguage: A graphics protocol must explain what happens when a person selects an object, not only how to draw it. It also needs to work with different kinds of displays.

sections.title: A Modular Software Design
sections.content:
The paper proposes building graphics support in levels, from basic terminal commands to higher-level programming languages, picture editors, data management and application programs. Each level should use services from lower levels and provide services to levels above it.

The author recommends designing the levels in parallel so experience with one can influence the others before their design becomes difficult to change.
sections.plainLanguage: The design has several levels, from hardware commands to applications. Each level builds on the one below it and supports the one above it.

sections.title: Picture Structure and User Input
sections.content:
The RFC describes pictures as directed structures of nodes and branches. A node can display lines or characters and call other nodes; a branch positions a called node and can set display parameters. This structure lets a shared subpicture be reused.

When a user points at an object, an application needs to know what was selected and receive related information. For storage-tube displays, the author recommends screen strips and a table of display pointers to identify the object under the input position.
sections.plainLanguage: A picture can be built from reusable parts linked together. When a person points at an item, the system should tell the application which part was selected.
